newsitem.title: USA: Regulators, states crack down on car lease ads.
newsitem.headline: Regulators, states crack down on car lease ads.

text.p: General Motors Corp. and four other automakers settled deceptive advertising charges by agreeing to spell out costs in their auto leasing ads, federal regulators said Thursday.

The crackdown by the Federal Trade Commission centred on ads that trumpeted "no money down" or "low monthly payment" terms in bold print, while putting other costs and sometimes contradictory information in small, often unreadable print.

The offices of 23 state attorneys general also settled with GM, Mitsubishi, Honda and Isuzu. The FTC said 15 states have filed complaints against Mazda. The automakers will pay a total of $1 million to reimburse the states' costs of investigating the complaints.

As a result, GM, Mitsubishi Motor Sales of America Inc., American Honda Motor Co., American Isuzu Motors Inc. and Mazda Motor of America Inc. will be required to change their ads to provide consumers with "clear, readable and understandable" information in their advertising.

"I saw one of these ads on television a while ago and I got down on my hands and knees in front of the TV set to try and read the fine print," FTC Chairman Robert Pitofsky said at a news conference. "Well, I couldn't."
Pitofsky said the settlement did not close the agency's investigation. "We are looking at ads from other companies."
Nearly one-third of new cars are now leased as the option continues to gain popularity among consumers.
Lincoln Merrihew, an automotive analyst with DRI/McGraw Hill in Cambridge, Mass., said clearer disclosure of "hidden" costs will help reduce the number of pitfalls for consumers.
"Ultimately this helps the consumer. Many people are overwhelmed with the simple purchase of vehicles, and leasing is even more complex," Merrihew said.
GM and Mitsubishi were also charged with misrepresenting financing terms in ads aimed at car buyers.

In one instance, a television ad for GM's Buick Regal touted that consumers could buy the vehicle for $2,000 down and 30 monthly payments of $249. But buried in scrolling and allegedly unreadable fine print was the disclosure that a final "balloon" payment was required, of $11,678.

A Mazda TV ad offering leases on four different models promoted low monthly payments and just "one penny down." The "unreadable" fine print, flashed briefly at the bottom of the screen, disclosed that at least $900 was due at the outset, along with taxes, title, license and registration fees.
"These rolling disclaimers are worthless," said Grant Woods, Arizona's attorney general. "If you need a disclaimer and you can't read the disclaimer, it's not a disclaimer."
Speaking at the FTC news conference, Woods said the ads were aimed at luring consumers to dealerships in the hopes that a deal could be struck once they arrive.
"Hopefully in the future, what they say is what you'll get," he said.
